newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul seeks detente with Pyongyang despite shooting.
newsitem.headline: Seoul seeks detente with Pyongyang despite shooting.

text.p: South Korea braced on Monday for possible attacks by Pyongyang but said confrontation over a high-level North Korean defector taking refuge at Seoul's embassy in Beijing would not scuttle its efforts for detente.

Another prominent defector, Li Il-nam, a nephew of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, remained in a coma after being critically wounded at the weekend by suspected North Korean agents near Seoul.
Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha said problems stemming from the defection in Beijing last week by Hwang Jang-yop were just the start of headaches for Seoul because of a crisis in the North.

"I believe the North Korean regime's crisis will deepen as time passes because there's no likelihood of improvement in its economic hardship and food shortages, and signs of laxity in its social order," Yoo told a meeting of South Korean diplomats.

South Korea's security-related ministers on Sunday agreed that a desperate North Korea could resort to guerrilla attacks after Hwang, a top adviser to North Korean leader Kim, sought asylum on Wednesday.
"We have drawn up a list of defectors, senior officials and politicians to provide tight security against any possible terrorist attacks by North Korea," a police officer told Reuters.
"Security around ports, airports and other public places has also been beefed up."
The precautionary steps were taken after Home Affairs Minister Suh Chung-hwa denounced the shooting of Li as "an assassination attempt by North Korean infiltrators".
Doctors said Li, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, was on a life support system on Monday and unlikely to regain consciousness.
About 10,000 police and soldiers searched for the two suspected North Korean agents who shot Li late on Saturday.
Foreign Minister Yoo said Seoul would step up efforts to hold peace talks with North Korea, along with the United States and China.
"To manage the fluid situation on the Korean peninsula... and maintain peace, we should achieve four-nation peace talks," he said.
The talks, proposed last year by Seoul and Washington, could include steps to reduce tensions on the divided peninsula and economic and other cooperation, he said.
A government spokesman said Seoul still wanted to join international efforts to provide food to famine-stricken North Korea despite the shooting incident.

"Cabinet ministers have confirmed our positions to take part in a new food aid progamme by an international body," he said, referring to a World Food Programme appeal for $41.6 million to buy 100,000 metric tonnes of aid. No more details were given.
In Beijing, Hwang spent his 74th birthday on Monday at the South Korean mission behind a fortress-like defence wall provided by Chinese security officials.
Pyongyang has said Hwang was kidnapped by Seoul, a claim brushed aside as preposterous by South Korea.
"If they make him go to Seoul, I think there will be war," said one Pyongyang official in Beijing.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry on Monday denied reports Hwang had met a U.S. intelligence official and had revealed plans by other Northern officials to flee. "No U.S. official has met Hwang Jang-yop," ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said.

State radio and local newspapers reported on Monday that Hwang had told an official from the Central Intelligence Agency that six or seven officials of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party wanted to seek political asylum.
